# Note: the Terminal panel (ghostty-web) on Windows

Asked 2026-11-17. Not tested on Windows: this is what should work, from reading the code and general
knowledge. A personal reference, not approved work.

## The idea

Use delulu-smash's Terminal panel (``Alt+` ``) from a Windows machine.

## What is known

- **ghostty-web** only draws the terminal, in the browser: it works in any Windows browser.
- **The shell behind it is the Linux-only part.** `services/ui/ui/terminal.py` uses Python's `pty` module and
  util-linux's `setsid`, and starts `$SHELL -l`. None of that exists on native Windows.
- **Ghostty the desktop app** has no Windows build. Its Linux build can run in WSL2 through WSLg, with rough
  edges (blurry high-DPI scaling, clipboard and font quirks, slower drawing). Windows Terminal or WezTerm are
  the usual native choices. Not needed for the panel.

## Ways to do it

| Way | How | Code change |
|---|---|---|
| **WSL2 (recommended)** | run the server in WSL (`ds ui run`), open `http://localhost:3000` in Edge / Chrome on Windows; the panel is the WSL shell | none expected |
| Native Windows | a ConPTY backend (eg the `pywinpty` package), starting PowerShell or `cmd` instead of `$SHELL` | yes: a second backend in `terminal.py` |

## Watch for

- The terminal only accepts connections from the same machine (`LOCAL_HOSTS`: `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`,
  `::1`; `allowed_origin`). WSL2 normally forwards `localhost` from Windows, so it should pass. If the panel
  stays blank, look there first; WSL's "mirrored" networking mode is the usual fix.

## Next steps (if this is ever wanted)

- Try the WSL2 way on a real Windows machine and record what happened here.
- Only then decide whether a native Windows backend is worth building.
